utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. May I introduce Ms. Colby Kuvara, who is from the San Francisco Bay Area, graduate of Hastings College of Law in San Francisco, is now completing her legal education here at the University of Leiden. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Edgerton. You have no seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm only here very briefly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We needed to quickly address a mischaracterisation based on an apparent misunderstanding that surfaced in yesterday's filing by the Defence in the motion to admit certain intercepts which indicated in part that the Prosecution, after reviewing its evidence collection, has agreed that the intercepts are authentic. As I indicated yesterday, of course, we did so with respect to a certain body of intercepts, but as I tried to make clear yesterday, not with respect to these. That is, there are certain factors here that distinguish this body of intercepts potentially from the others so that agreement has not been reached. I'm happy to explain or indeed have Ms. Edgerton explain in greater deal the issues underlying that distinction but that would have to be done in private session because they involve the methodology. But what I can say in open session is that I have communicated to Mr. Robinson that the understanding upon which his motion was premised is not accurate, that we consider that these intercepts or at least the vast bulk of them need to be authenticated with the evidence of the appropriate witness. I believe that 30 intercepts were the subject of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Prosecution is going to file a response?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will. I just -- but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the Chamber will not issue its decision until it hears from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then that's -- that's fine. That's mainly the purpose of my intervention at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But when could the Chamber see your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. As far as I'm concerned, if the Prosecution has -- if they don't agree to authentication, then we will have to call the witness. I don't think there is any need for the Chamber to make any decision on that point. So -- we believed erroneously that we had an agreement, but I didn't understand Mr. Tieger clearly enough, so there is no agreement with respect to the Croatian intercepts. Therefore the only issue left is for us to schedule the witness. There's nothing that the Chamber needs to decide. They have the perfect right to insist on authentication by the witness and we don't have any problem with them exercising that right. In fact, they have been more than accommodating to us on this issue. So I was going to propose to file an amended notice to the Croatian government to schedule the testimony of that witness for the 3rd of March at 4.00 p.m. and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The Chamber hadn't enough time to read the Defence motion itself. So it's for you to file an additional motion, but let us wait till the Chamber reads the Prosecution's response in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And I just -- we will endeavour to make that as quickly as possible, Mr. President, rather than obviously exhaust the full amount of time that otherwise might be available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would appreciate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we bring in the next witness. Mr. Mudrinic? Yes, Mudrinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mudrinic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Mudrinic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the Tribunal. That is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges, if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you, and, as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Mudrinic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mudrinic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to kindly appeal to you, just as I do to all the Serbian speakers, that we have to speak slowly for the sake of the record. Mr. Mudrinic, have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 1D49500.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the Serbian version of your statement, page 1 on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown the last page, please, so that he may identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the statement faithfully reflect your words to the Defence team? Are the facts correct or does anything need rectifying?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Everything is just as I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask you the same questions today as were put to you when the statement was taken, would your answers be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender the statement into evidence under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. McKenna, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4387, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out in English a short summary of the statement of Mr. Dusan Mudrinic. [In English] Dusan Mudrinic was a member of the Serbian Defence Forces known as the SOS, which was a unit of the 6th Sana Brigade. He was a member of the SDS and lived in Sanski Most. After the breakup of the SFRY, Muslims started buying weapons illegally and prepared for war. The SOS was formed after Muslim extremists provoked the first incident at the check-point that they set up in Trnava village. The SOS was created because of the need to look out for the civilians, who feared for their safety since the 6th Sana Brigade was on the front in Croatia and the JNA was pulling out to Serbia. Although the Serbian authorities offered the Croats and the Muslims to divide the town into Serbian and Muslim parts, municipality, Muslim extremists entered the Sanski Most municipal building with the goal to creating the Muslim police and Territorial Defence of BH in -- for the entire city. After their refusal to comply with the ultimatum to surrender their weapons and leave the building, the Serbian authorities issued an order to the Territorial Defence and parts of the Serbian police to disarm this group and free the municipal building. Soon after, the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most municipality called on all the citizens of the area to surrender to the Territorial Defence and the civilian police all the weapons that they had in their possessions illegally. Since some Muslim extremists in the Mahala neighbourhood refused to comply, the Command of the 6th Sana Brigade received the task to enter Mahala, identify the extremists, and hand them over to the law enforcement authorities. After all the incidents provoked by the Muslim extremists and the setting up of check-points in each village, telephone lines were cut, there were power cuts, and the traffic to neighbouring towns was disrupted. Some individuals and groups took advantage of the situation by engaging in looting and committing crimes, but the Serbian authorities tried to bring the situation under control and started proceedings against the perpetrators of crimes. The loyal and honest people of Sanski Most were not brought in, maltreated or interrogated, no matter what religion. A number of Muslims from surrounding villages who did not want conflict the Serbian authorities asked to gather in the sports hall in Sanski Most for their own security. Simultaneously, Serbian refugees started arriving from all over BH after being driven out of towns taken over by Muslim forces. The municipal authorities received the Serbian refugees and tried to accommodate them in houses abandoned by people who had already left voluntarily. The Serbian authorities did their best to help with the organisation of convoys and security of the people who decided to leave the municipality. Nonetheless, about 5.000 Muslims continued to live and work in the Sanski Most from 1992 to 1995, which shows that the Serbian authorities conducted a fair and reasonable policy towards all people, regardless of their ethnicity. Dr. Karadzic could not know what was happening on the ground every moment, especially at the time when communication lines were cut off. When the lines were restored, he insisted on ensuring peace and security for all people. Dr. Karadzic did not take part in crimes or instigated the permanent removal of the Bosnian Muslims and Croats from the territory to which Serbs laid claims, at least concerning my municipality. The Serbian authorities gave the Muslims and the Croats the chance to stay and live freely in the Republika Srpska as long as they respected the constitution and the laws of the Republika Srpska. And that is the short summary. At that moment, I do not have additional questions for Mr. Mudrinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Mudrinic, your evidence in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written statement, in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the -- of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, your nickname was Medeni; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And Dusan Saovic, to whom you refer in your statement, his nickname was Njunja?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Njunja. That was it. Not Ninja.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And Njunja was the SOS commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: You were his deputy; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to name some other members of the SOS. I want you to confirm either yes or no whether they were members of the SOS. Firstly, Vojo Dusenovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Vojo Dosenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Was he a member of the SOS, Mr. Mudrinic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member of the SOS.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Milan Camber also known as Skica, was he a member of the SOS?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Milan Camber aka Skica.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Was Milan Camber a member of the SOS, Mr. Mudrinic, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was but just for a period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Goran Kerkes, was he a member of the SOS?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Goran Kerkes was not a member of the SOS.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: What about Zoran Bubulj?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: He was not a member.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And Danilusko Kajtez?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Danilusko Kajtez was a member for some two months or two months and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 4 of your statement, you say: "The SDS had nothing do with our establishment. Our SOS and the SOS from Banja Luka had nothing to do with each other." It's true, though, isn't it, Mr. Mudrinic, that when formally establishing the SOS Sanski Most, you liaised with the authorities of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: It's true that when the SOS was established we liaised with the Territorial Defence of Sanski Most because we were former members of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter number 26051.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, you'll see that this is a proclamation of the Serb Defence Forces Staff of the Serb municipality of Sanski Most. And it's signed the SOS. And it's dated the 13th of April, 1992. And in the first paragraph it states: "We hereby inform the Serb people and the general public of the Serb municipality of Sanski Most that a unit of the Serb Defence Forces (SOS) was formed on the 12th of April in Lusci Palanka." First thing, Mr. Mudrinic, do you agree that the formation of a unit of the SOS suggests that it is a unit of a larger organisation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I don't agree that it belonged to a larger organisation. The SOS was established in Sanski Most in that -- in Luska Palanka --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat what he said last.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, the interpreter did not hear your final sentence. If you could just repeat from -- you say that it was formed on the 12th -- I'm sorry. You said the SOS was established in Luska Palanka. Was there anything else that you wanted to add?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: It was established in Sanski Most but its establishment was proclaimed or announced in Luska Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at the fifth paragraph of this document, which states: "The insignia of [sic] and the uniforms of the unit were designed on the basis of an agreement with the JNA and the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina ..." So you'll agree, Mr. Mudrinic, that this shows the SOS liaising with both the JNA and the ARK at its formation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: That what's the proclamation says. When it was established, the JNA insignia were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6680, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mudrinic, the Trial Chamber has heard from your fellow SOS member Vinko Nikolic, who testified that he was appointed as the SOS representative on the Crisis Staff at a meeting on the 14th of April, 1992. It's true, isn't it, that the SOS worked closely with the SDS in the Serb take-over of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: That's true. With the proviso that we did not interfere with the authorities. We didn't organise anything. We only helped the enforcement of all the legal provisions. And it is true that Vinko Nikolic was a representative, but we helped it be implemented in accordance with the law. I mean the take-over. That's true. We did not interfere with the authority as such. We only assisted in the process.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter number 26053.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This is a report on the activities and the participation in combat of the SOS as per the plan of the 6th Krajina Brigade and it's dated 4th September 1992. And if we look it explains that the SOS was formed and placed under the command of the 6th Brigade and then it states: "All actions to date" -- this in the third paragraph down. "All actions to date have been carried out with the approval of the brigade command. Since the establishment of the 6th Brigade, the members of the SOS have carried out many important tasks and activities as the members of the Sanski Most SOS." And it details those activities: Transporting and disseminating weaponry, presence in the theatre of war. It details the capturing of the municipality building, all of the mopping up actions in the territory of the municipality. So is this a fair reflection of how the SOS assisted in the process, as you've just explained?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: The only thing that is correct is that we patrolled. We checked the movement of suspicious individuals and thus prevent the activities of terrorist groups. And as for preventing HDZ and SDA members in terrorist actions, those terrorist actions did not exist in Sanski Most. There were no terrorist actions at all for that matter. If we have in mind the same terrorist actions. There were certain activities but not terrorist activities, not activities of that nature, on any of the sides. Patrolling meant that we helped people in the nearby villages. We would boost their morale by telling them that when they erected barricades or when they held village guards that they should not participate in incidents. If they thought that an incident might occur, that they should inform competent bodies, and that's what we told them. Nothing else. The distribution of arms, no. We never brought any arms to our area. We never distributed any arms to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, we'll come on to the specifics of the activity of the SOS in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6681, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: But I'd like to just focus for the moment on your relationship between -- your relationship with the Crisis Staff. In your statement at paragraph 4 you say that you placed yourself under the command of the TO and then you've explained that you were later subordinated to the 6th Brigade. That's in paragraph 8. You received payment from the Crisis Staff, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I've never heard of those monies before. I don't think I received anything. If anything was received, it was not a salary. It was just a -- a minor financial aid for bare necessities. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter number 26052.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This is a -- these are the conclusions of a Crisis Staff meeting held on the 16th of June, 1992. And I'd like to focus your attention on item number 3, which states: "Anicic submitted a report on the work of the military police and the activity of Njunja's sabotage platoon called," and there's a word crossed out. That's a reference to Nedjo Anicic, the TO commander, reporting on the SOS, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: It is true that Anicic was TO commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 4, it states: "Crisis Staff approved the financial assistance (a reward for the sabotage platoon and a platoon of military police in the amount of a daily subsistence allowance of 1.500 dinars)." So this document shows the commander Anicic reporting to the Crisis Staff on the activities of the SOS and the Crisis Staff approving financial assistance to the SOS; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm reading, but I never received that financial assistance. And if we did receive anything, like I have just told you, it was just assistance for bare necessities or assistance in kind. I -- I'm not aware of this particular financial assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if I am seeing things well but I would like to see an explanation. I don't see here a reference to the SOS or, rather, that the group was known under that name. Am I missing something here?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The witness has just confirmed that the reference to Njunja's sabotage platoon is a reference to the SOS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question was about paragraph 4. Paragraph 4, 5, 6, whether it has any reference to the SOS group. But you can read it. The document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6682, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mudrinic, you just -- we just saw a document where Njunja stated that the SOS transported and disseminated weaponry. You have just claimed that you never distributed arms and that contrasts with the testimony of Mr. Nikolic who told this Trial Chamber that the SOS helped to arm the Serbian people in Sanski Most before the conflict broke out. Now -- I'm sorry, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that at all. That we, as a platoon, disseminated weapons, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, out of abundance of caution, I'd like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that from 1991 you were bringing weapons from the Prijedor military barracks to Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Not true. In 1991, I was never in the Prijedor barracks. Neither in 1991 nor 1992. I don't know what (redacted) had in mind when he said that. He should be here to tell you all that. I was never in the Prijedor barracks in 1991. We never transported weapons in any kind of cars. There were indicia that things of that kind were being done. However, the civilian police stopped people on two or three occasions, myself, the late Saovic. They controlled the vehicles. They never found anything. They searched us. They searched the vehicle. They never found any weapons. They never found anything. Now why would anybody say this, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's come on to talk about some of your other pre-war activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I note that a line perhaps need to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last part of the answer. The witness didn't say, "Now why would anybody say that, I don't know." He didn't say "anybody." He said, "Why would he say that, I don't know."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, and other SOS members were trained in handling explosives. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's look at your own statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: That's 65 ter number 25968.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, this is a statement that you gave on the 22nd of December, 1992. You gave it to the Sanski Most police regarding the matter of Njunja's death which had taken place earlier that month.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm interested in page 5 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S, please. I think we appear to have ... we -- we appear to have the wrong document. I'm interested in 65 ter number 25968.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you state --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we have the previous page in the English briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: At the very bottom you say -- of the English you say: "I saw the place where Njunja was lying down and the injuries he had sustained and, in my opinion, and I have been trained in handling explosives, it could have been that the explosive was thrown at the moment Njunja was passing the vehicle. In answer to the question whether the SOS unit members still have their explosives with them, since I have mentioned that they have been trained in handling explosives, I state that I do not know whether they had it with them." So I'll ask you again, Mr. Mudrinic, it's true, isn't it, that you and the other SOS members had been trained in handling explosives?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: My answer is the same. We were never trained in handling explosives. I, as a soldier in the former JNA, was a member of such a unit where I was supposed to be familiar with explosives, but that was in 1975. Perhaps that's the reason why I said that I could handle explosives. But for any specific training during the relevant period of time, no, we didn't have any. It's not correct that we were trained in handling explosives.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you going to refer to this statement further or --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What page was it --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- page 4?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: -- pages 4 and 5 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit those two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6683, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, it's true, isn't it, that even before the conflict broke out, the SOS were notorious for blowing up buildings belonging to non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of any such explosions that could have blown up buildings in Sanski Most. It is not true that they did that in Sanski Most. And as for an explosion that could blow up a building, honestly, there were no such explosions at all. In the majority of the cases, if there was an explosion, and if we could call them that, it would be a -- a bomb that exploded but that explosion was of a much lesser extent. There was no such an explosion in Sanski Most that could have blown up a building, an entire building.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, there's evidence before this Trial Chamber of SOS bombings of Muslim- and Croat-owned buildings in 1991 and early 1992, including law offices, cafe bars, and other buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And for the parties' reference, that's KDZ474, P3395, pages 10 to 19; KDZ490, P3634, pages 31 to 32.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: You and Njunja personally placed these bombs, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: It is not true that I and the late Saovic placed those bombs. I repeat what I've just told you: There were no explosions that could blow up buildings. There were explosions that damaged buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you were responsible for those explosions, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I repeat: We didn't do that. But let me emphasise once again, the police controlled us on several occasions. They checked us, and those were police members of both Serb and Muslim ethnicity, and they never found any weapons or explosives on us. None of the searches of our vehicles or of -- or our bodies revealed anything. There were explosions, but I don't know who was responsible for that. Those explosions usually took place at night. But I don't know who was responsible. And, also, I'd like to say that Serbian buildings were blown up as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The truth is that no real efforts were made to find those people responsible because the Serb authorities blocked any investigations. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: The Serb authorities did try to find the perpetrators. In Serbian public security stations there were also Muslims who worked on that. They were mixed patrols when people and facilities were searched. They tried but they failed. I don't know why they failed. But they worked together, both Serbs and Muslims who were affiliated with the public security station. I repeat: Things like that usually happened at night, and they couldn't cover the entire territory to make sure that things were done successfully.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On line 19, it has been translated as "Serb buildings were also blown up," and the witness said -- said: Serb facilities were blown up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, the people who you confirmed earlier were SOS member, Milan Camber, Danilusko Kajtez, these people were known criminals, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: There were no criminals in -- there were -- there was no crime in Sanski Most and there were even fewer criminals. I can't say that they were criminals. People saw everything. But I don't think that they were criminals. I don't think so. You should open their files and you should see whether they have criminal records. I don't know. There was no crime. There were no criminals in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: At least not to a large extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to refer the parties to D4351 and the testimony of KW545 at T 46964 to 46966.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: But, Mr. Mudrinic, I'd like to show you the testimony of Adil Draganovic, who was the president of the Sanski Most Court before the war, and he testified at some length in another trial before this Tribunal regarding the SOS.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 26047. Unfortunately, we don't have a B/C/S version of this, but I will read it out slowly. He was asked when he first heard of the SOS. And he states: "It's hard for me to define precisely at the time, but I can say that I first heard about some secret Serb organisation who were civilians and that they were rather prone to criminal behaviour, of [sic] setting up of explosives, mining, provoking disorder. I knew most of these people." Could we please skip forward to page 3. And halfway down the page he's asked: "What sort of reputation did these people have? And he responds: "They were mostly problematic persons, meaning their behaviour. I can say that they were criminals, in fact."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So you've just told us there was no crime in Sanski Most, no crime to speak of, and yet here is a judge from the court of Sanski Most describing you and your colleagues as criminals.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I don't know how can I answer the question. I don't know even who the judge is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat what he said last.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, could you please repeat the end of your answer. You said you don't know who the judge is. Did you have anything else to add?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I don't know if that's the judge, Ankica Dobrijevic, the judge who described us here as criminals -- well, what I can say is that I'm 57 now and never in my life have I had a criminal report filed against me, and I have never been convicted, of course. So if a judge described me as a criminal, then just on that account it must be right. I have not been brought before a single court in Bosnia-Herzegovina for any offence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's see what this judge said about you personally, Mr. Mudrinic. He goes on to describe how --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Excuse me. Can we ask the Prosecutor to tell the witness whose statement this is? Because obviously the witness doesn't understand which judge is involved here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think she mentioned Adil Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, he mentioned another name, but it's Adil Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as for Adil Draganovic, that judge, what I can say, in addition to the fact that I have never been prosecuted, is that he may have been involved in crime. When I arrived in Banja Luka, I was informed by him, this is something that arrived to my address of residence, that he as the president of the court in Sanski Most issued an injunction against me on any sale of immovable property.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic -- Mr. Mudrinic, I -- perhaps Mr. Karadzic will like to go into this in this re-direct. I'd like to focus right now on what Mr. Draganovic said about you in his testimony before another Chamber of this Tribunal. He's asked -- and this is in the next page. He describes the fact that your group were terrorising the town, provoking fear among the population and every night they were blowing up a building belonging to Bosniaks. And he's asked: "What about attacks on people? Did they carry out attacks on people as well?" And he says: "Yes, absolutely. They also attacked people. On one occasion, I was in a situation when a teacher called me on the phone, a secondary ... teacher from Sanski Most grammar school. His name was Blaz Grgic. He was a teacher of German. He told me that his apartment had been broken into and that he been robbed, that he was robbed of a large sum of money, and that he had -- he was -- he told me that this was done by two persons whose names were Dusan Saovic, aka Njunja, and Dusan Mudrinic, aka Medeni, who already then were feared in town, together with other members of that group. He did not dare report it to the police ... at that time. So I called him to come with [sic] with me and I interviewed him. "After that interview, I had reasonable grounds to believe these persons did commit this offence. I then reported this to the police, and I ordered for this to be investigated. However, the following day, that is ... they went into the school centre with weapons. They were armed. And they attacked the teacher, who was then forced to flee ... Sanski Most either the next day or the following days." Mr. Mudrinic, you personally attacked and intimidated non-Serbs, including this school teacher, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. All the non-Serb population, and I state this under full responsibility, of all the military and the authorities, it was the late Saovic and I that they placed most of the trust in. They were not attacked in the street. None of the Muslims who stayed behind in Sanski Most were ever harmed. What's more, they even socialised with us. As for this Professor Blaz, it is true that he accused Saovic and I, that we broke into his apartment and stole his effects. This case ended up in the public security station. They attended the scene, carried out on an on-site investigation and established that the flat was not broken into at all, that the lock had not been forced or anything of the sort. Later on, in certain circles he confessed that he had given the money that he claimed was stolen to the party but he couldn't admit this to his wife. It's true that -- it's not true that Saovic and I went chasing after him with weapons. We never carried weapons in town. It was only on rare occasions. We would normally walk about the town in civilian clothes and without weapons, and this is something that all the Muslims who stayed behind in Sanski Most can attest to. So I do not agree with the statement given here by this man, Blaz. What can you think of a man who claims to have had his apartment burgled and then when police come to inspect the scene, they find out that the lock had not been forced, that none of the windows had been forced, so how can the flat have been broken into?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: It was because of this -- I'm sorry. It was because of this that I was taken to court. The court established that, on the facts of the case, the apartment could not have been broken into and all the charges were dropped.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: You've referred to the Muslims who stayed behind and we'll come on to discuss that. But in paragraph 13 of your statement, you say that even before the outbreak of the conflict, Muslims had begun to move out of the municipality. That was precisely your aim in the SOS, wasn't it, to terrorise Muslims into leaving the municipality?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: In which way we could have terrorised Muslims, I don't think we did. As for people we knew better personally, we told them they didn't need to leave the city, that proper government will be established, that life would come to normal again. In any case, we didn't drive them away. On the contrary, we tried to persuade them to stay. And it was them who wished to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see P3397.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, you've said that there was no crime to speak of in Sanski Most and you've said that you were -- the SOS certainly wasn't involved in any explosions. I'll like to see what Njunja and your fellow SOS members stated. This is a report on the work and activities of the SOS between the 1st of May and 16th of September -- excuse me, the 1st of May, 1991, and the 16th of September, 1992. And Mr. Nikolic confirmed to this Trial Chamber that it was signed by Njunja, Cankovic, and himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see page 2 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S. It's the second paragraph in the B/C/S and the second-last paragraph on the page in the English and it states: "We never allowed large gatherings of SDA and HDZ to take place at any stage, and we broke up any such gathering in the usual way. The SDS from Sanski Most is our witness that we put them into power. It's unbearable to think that what could have happened if we had not acted in this way. Blowing up buildings was not in anyone's interest, but we could not crush the Ustashas and the Green Berets any other way."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And that's the truth, isn't it, Mr. Mudrinic, the SOS blew up buildings owned by Muslims and Croats and attacked the non-Serb population in order to sow fear among that population and intimidate them into leaving the municipality?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Partially I cannot -- in fact, I cannot agree with this because, again, reference is made to the blowing up of buildings and everything, and these explosions that happened were not major explosions. Those were perhaps hand-grenades that were thrown. I'd like to emphasise that nobody was hurt or wounded or killed by these hand-grenades. As for intimidation, I don't know what they consider to be intimidation. If we appeared in a certain place when we had an advance report that they would gather and we showed up there to stop it, maybe that was their thinking.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The SOS used a truck with a triple-barrelled machine-gun mounted on it, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you and Njunja were in charge of operating that truck?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: That's not true. Not -- not true. That truck had a driver. It had a triple-barrelled gun, but we used it to drive from one place to another. And this triple-barrelled gun was -- in fact this truck was used mainly to transport personnel and troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It was also used, Mr. Mudrinic, wasn't it, it was also used to fire indiscriminately on civilian houses in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: In Mahala, this triple-barrelled gun was not fired at all until the end of the operation in Mahala. When the operation was finished, that triple-barrelled gun fired only at the forest, the direction where these Muslim extremists had fled. Only at the very end. And in Mahala, it never opened fire at houses or anything. And I have to emphasise that such a truck existed also in one unit from Usti Palanka [phoen]. This truck never opened fire. Only at the end of everything it fired at the forest where the extremists from Mahala had fled.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Actually, at paragraph 11 -- 11 and 20 of your statement, you say that people came to the collection centres of their own free will for protection. And you say at paragraph 19 that you don't know that loyal, honest people of Sanski Most municipality were brought in, maltreated or interrogated. Now witnesses have described before this Trial Chamber, Muslim witnesses have described men, women, and children being rounded up and brought to the detention centres, including Krings Hall and the sports hall, and either detained there or transported out of the municipality. And these witnesses described how they didn't choose to go there. They were rounded up and detained under armed guard. That's the reality of what was happening, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: The reality of what happened is that after this operation in Mahala, the Muslims who lived in Mahala wanted to be in one place, not to be scattered across various streets, and this sports hall was chosen. It was not a closed facility. It was open. They were able to go home and visit. They were able to go do some shopping, but the civilian police was there to provide security. And I don't know that anybody took anybody else outside of town. As for this Krings Hall, I've never been there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The SOS assisted the SJB in taking Muslims and Croats into custody. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And -- for instance, you, Mr. Mudrinic, led the group of men who arrested Mirzet Karabeg, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I was there and I remember clearly. I never detained him, nor did I take him for an interview. I was just passing by when his sister, who used to be my teacher of Serbian, told me that I was responsible for him, and I said, Why should I be responsible? I'm just taking him for an interview. But I didn't take him anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg testified in this case that on the 25th of May, 1992, he was arrested by two vehicles full of eight armed individuals and taken to the police station. And that's at P3303, page 73. Now, he gave more details on his arrest at -- in his testimony in the Krajisnik case. And I'm going to read to you what he said in that case. He said: "I was arrested at home, and it was the people that I just identified," and he had listed Dusan Mudrinic, Dusko Savija, Tomo Delic, Dane Kajtez, "it was the people I had just identified that arrested me. They were led by Dusan Mudrinic, also known as Medeni." And he's asked: "Where did they take you?" And he responds: "They took me to the police station. Medeni told me that Rasula and other police officers wanted to see me and have an interview with me." So it's not the truth is it, Mr. Mudrinic, that you were just simply passing by? You were leading the group of men who arrested Mr. Karabeg and you did so on the instructions of Crisis Staff president, Rasula.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I maintain here that I never detained or arrested Mirzet Karabeg. All I know is that outside the building of the SUP his sister told me I was responsible for him. I said, Why would be I responsible? I'm not the executive authorities, I'm nothing. Why I would be responsible? I was not the law. I was not enforcing the law. I only assisted in certain times when there was not enough police. And I didn't go there voluntarily, only when I was summoned. They told me: You know, we don't have enough men. Can you give us three or four men to help the civilian police? The civilian police did the detaining and we were there just to provide some security so as to avoid incidents. I was not executive authority. I was just a simple soldier who provided assistance whenever that was required. As for explaining things to people why they need to go for an interview, that was all done by civilian policemen. I was there to prevent incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Mudrinic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Mudrinic, do you agree that you assisted or provided some security when police arrested Mr. Karabeg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was I assisting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's what you said. You assisted on some certain -- on certain times. And you referred to providing security. So my question is whether you provided security when civilian police arrested Mr. Karabeg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 32, line 5. What is recorded is exactly opposite to what the witness said. The witness said: I did not take him in for an interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I think that should be corrected. You agree, Mr. Mudrinic, having said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never took that man in for an interview. I was not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's talk about the type of assistance that the SOS members were providing to the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript. The witness didn't say, I wasn't there. He just said, on that occasion, he did not bring him in. Line 4. And I would like to ask the witness to speak slowly and to enunciate in order to avoid this confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Mudrinic, with Mr. Karadzic's comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Witnesses, Mr. Mudrinic, witnesses have described the beatings that took place at Sanski Most police building, including by your SOS colleague, Danilusko Kajtez. You knew these beatings were taking place, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: My task as an assistant to the civilian police was to bring that man for an interview. When my task was over and I left, what was done by inspectors in the public security station, how they were interrogated, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So let me just clarify your testimony, Mr. Mudrinic. You -- do you accept that you brought Mr. Karabeg in for an interview?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I do not accept that. I know on three occasions I operated as assistant to the civilian police. I know the names and surnames of these people whom I assisted, with whom I assisted. And, as for Mirzet Karabeg, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you say you didn't know of the beatings that were taking place at the SJB. Did you know of the beatings that were taking place at the Betonirka facility by -- conducted by SOS members, including, again, Mr. Kajtez. Were you aware of those beatings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat once again: Concerning the beatings at the public security station, I didn't know about that because I was not there. Concerning the beatings in Betonirka, I heard there had been beatings but I had nothing do with it whatsoever. I was not the warden. I wasn't anything. I heard about it, but I wasn't present and I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 8 again. It says after the words "Mirzet Karabeg," "I don't know." The witness said: "I didn't," not "I don't know." Perhaps we can listen to the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness is speaking very inarticulately, in addition to very fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, do you confirm that you said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break and resume -- continue at 11.00. But, Mr. Mudrinic, could you speak much slower when we resume so that the interpreters can understand you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, you and your SOS colleagues facilitated the transfer of detainees from Sanski Most to Manjaca camp. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: It is correct that seven -- six or seven or eight of our members - I don't know how many exactly - co-operated with the police, and they assisted the police. They were aboard the buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: An eye-witness, Sakib Muhic, saw your SOS colleagues Milan Camber and Danilusko Kajtez beat six men to death outside the Manjaca camp. Were you aware of that incident?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, it's a fact, isn't it, that the SOS not only rounded up Serbs -- non-Serbs and brought them into detention, its members also participated in the mistreatment and killings that occurred in the detention camps?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: The SOS members were not in detention camps -- camps at all. I repeat: They were only on the escort of the buses on the way to the camps. I know for a fact that they did not linger in the camp. They were only there on the way to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: In paragraph 10 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 14, the previous page, it says they were aboard buses. Whereas he said they were aboard the buses, one each. Assisting the police. So one was on each of the buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Mudrinic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: In paragraph 10 of your statement, you say that after the conflict broke out, some individuals and groups took advantage of that situation by engaging in looting and some crimes were committed, but the Serbian authorities tried to put a stop to that situation and bring it under control as soon as possible. Now, Mr. Mudrinic, in your statement of the 22nd of December, 1992, you refer to your cafe Leli. That cafe was forcibly taken from Muslim Reuf Sadic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: What I can say about this is that it's not true that the cafe was forcefully seized. The Muslim's name is Eko Sadic. I was a permanent guest in that cafe, and I was on very friendly terms with this Muslim. His wife is a Serb, so they were in a mixed marriage. They used to live in Switzerland. She stayed behind and he returned of his own initiative. Or, actually, it was at his own initiative that the two of us went to a lawyer, Panic, where we drew up a contract on the basis of which I would take over his cafe. After I had taken his cafe over, the man did not leave. He would stay in the cafe as before, and his security or safety wasn't threatened. So it is not true that it was seized from him. It was at his own initiative that we drew up the papers at a lawyer's. It wasn't just the cafe. There was a dwelling unit above the cafe. So I repeat: It's not true that it was seized from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Njunja took the Gold Cafe from a Muslim goldsmith, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Equally, the owner, Fikret Zlatar, gifted or gave the cafe over to Saovic. After he did this, he stayed in Sanski Most for a while. So he didn't leave right away. And, again, it was not forcefully taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Goran Cankovic, another SOS member, his Spider cafe also used to belong to a Muslim, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Goran Cankovic had a cafe of his own. The owner of the cafe Spider was his very close friend who similarly handed the cafe over to him. And he also frequented the cafe later and stayed there. There were also instances where cafes would be rented out by the municipality or would be handed over by friends. What I can state for these specific cases is that the cafes in question had not been forcefully taken. What's more, the owner of the cafe that I kept, at one point said that he wanted to go out to visit his wife. He decided that he should leave, though I tried to persuade him against it, but I placed him on the bus, and I spoke to him on the phone later when he was in Germany. His wife came back during the war. I gave her the keys to the apartment upstairs. She wanted to collect her belongings. She was glad [Realtime transcript read in error "blad"] that it had not been damaged or that it had not been taken up by anyone else and then she went. So the owner, when returned from Germany to Sanski Most, he telephoned me and we spoke. There were no problems. So they were not forcibly taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, you sold --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 1, page 39, "she was blad," it says. He said that she was happy to see that it had not been damaged and was grateful for it. I don't know what "blad" is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a -- I think it's a typo of "glad." Happy and glad. Yes. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Vojo Dosenovic's cafe, Cobra, that also used to belong to a Muslim, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that cafe. I can't remember the cafe Cobra.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So all these cafes that were gifted by Muslims to you and your SOS colleagues, your own cafe, you sold that on -- at a profit, your own profit, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: That's not true. As for the cafe that I kept, since there was no combat in that area, the cafe was renovated by the owner's own brother, who lived next door. He was a valued businessman in Sanski Most. A carpenter. He spoke to his brother in Germany, and at my initiative, he renovated the cafe. His brother would sit with me there. I didn't sell it to anyone. I didn't give it to anyone. When I left Sanski Most, the cafe stayed behind in nobody's ownership -- or, actually, in the ownership of what was properly the rightful owner.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: You and your SOS colleagues drove around in cars appropriated from Muslims, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: There were cars that had been taken from Muslims, but there were also cars which were, just like the cafes, gifted to friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, you mentioned in your statement the mosques which were destroyed. You and your SOS colleagues were among those who blew them up, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: That's not true. We didn't blow up mosques.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The truth is, Mr. Mudrinic, that it was your group that you say the authorities were trying to control, and yet they weren't controlled. They weren't controlled because they were operating hand in hand with the authorities. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I cannot agree with the statement that the authorities could not keep us under control because we were available at the disposal of the authorities 24/7. We were all in a hall in downtown Sanski Most, up -- upstairs from us there was a radio device [as interpreted], so we were there, present, at the disposal of the authorities, and they could always get in touch with us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that the witness said something about the phones that we didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, you said -- can you repeat what you said about phones.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. There were no telephone lines. There was no communication. The majority of our members, of the members of our unit, lived some 5, 6, or 7 kilometres away from the town proper, in the neighbouring villages. So that if the authorities needed us at some point, we wouldn't be able to get in touch with them. That's why we decided, together with the authorities, that all of us should spend nights in the centre of town in a building, in the sports hall, where they would always be able to contact us. So it's not true that they weren't able to have us under control.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 18, page 40, it says "radio device," whereas it should read "the Sanski Most radio station."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Hmm. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, you've -- in your statement, you repeatedly refer -- and again today you have repeatedly referred to Muslims leaving Sanski Most voluntarily and of their own free will. And you say that the fact that around 5.000 Muslims continued to live and work in Sanski Most from 1992 to 1995 shows that the Serbian authorities conducted a fair and reasonable policy towards all people, regardless of their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, Arkan and his men arrived in Sanski Most in September 1995. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation we received was that this was in September 1992, so that's what the witness heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'll ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Arkan and his men arrived in Sanski Most in September 1995. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you personally assisted Arkan's men in rounding up non-Serbs and bringing them in for interrogation. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. I didn't have anything in common with Arkan and his formations, save for this one moment, when our own authorities appealed to us to find cattle for food. At one point, a colleague showed up, Predrag Dosenovic, who said that some seven or eight sheep were left with him by some farmers and they were transferred to Arkan's headquarters because there was butcher there among his men who was supposed to slaughter them. So that was it. Other than that, I didn't have anything to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter number 26032.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: While this is coming up, Mr. Mudrinic, four witnesses gave statements to the ICTY describing how, together with Arkan's men, you abducted them, beat them, threw them into a boot of a car and brought them for interrogation. We're going to look at just one of these statements now. Unfortunately, we don't have a B/C/S version of this statement but we'll go through it slowly. It's English page 3, and this is the statement of Zecir Sadic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. Did you say that I had beaten somebody and that I had put him in a car trunk? Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: We're going to be going through this statement in detail and then I'll put my question to you. This is what this witness says about an incident that occurred in late September 1995. And he stated: "I was looking for a relative to stay with when I saw Dusan Mudrinic, a local Serb, about 30 to 32 years. He was in the first of two cars that were driving in convoy. He shouted out to me "stop" and got out of the car. As he did so, four soldiers who were dressed in the same way as the soldiers who had been at my house the previous evening jumped out of the following car. Mudrinic was acting as a guide for these soldiers. He was pointing out where Muslims were living. "When these soldiers jumped out of the car, I realised that they were Arkan's men because of their appearance and the fact that they were strangers to the area." And he goes on to describe the beatings that he and another individual sustained at the hands of these soldiers and then he states: "When they were finished beating Smajo, they forced both of us into the boot of one of the cars head first. This resulted in our legs protruding from the boot of the car and the boot lid not being closed. Before being forced into the car boot, I was aware that there were two people in the other car boot in the same manner as us. We were driven off." Now, do you recall this incident, Mr. Mudrinic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, all of the victims of this incident corroborate this story in detailed statements to the ICTY. They state that you were driving around with Arkan's men in convoy, pointing out Muslims, beating them up, throwing them into the boots of cars, and bringing them to the headquarters of Arkan's men for interrogation. And that's the truth, isn't it? You personally abducted Muslims, beat them, and delivered them into the hands of Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: This is not correct. And I claim with full responsibility that from 1992 to 1995, I didn't beat a single Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let look at one more statement relating to an incident that occurred during the same period.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do you know this -- this gentleman, Zecir Sadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know the man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter number 26034. This is another ICTY statement. This time of Fatima Omic. If we could go to page 2 of the English, towards the bottom of the -- the page. And she has described how she heard about Arkan's take-over of Sanski Most on the radio. And then she states: "Later, two uniformed soldiers came to our house, being guided by Dusan Mudrinic." If we go to the next page. "They came into our house and told my husband, Taib Omic, to get dressed and to follow them. Taib did not argue. He just did what he was told and went with them. I did not see my husband alive again after that. I was then expelled from my house to the village of Sehovici. Over the next few days, I made a nuisance of myself trying to find out what happened to my husband. But no one would give me any information. "I heard nothing more about my husband until they exhumed the mass grave at Sasina in July 1996. I identified his body in the temporary mortuary set up at Krings factory. I recognised him by the clothing he was wearing. It was impossible for me to recognise any facial features because of the damage that had been caused to his head."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, this is an account of a 64-year-old woman, Mr. Mudrinic, describing how you assisted Arkan's men in the abduction of her husband. Do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that incident. I claim that I didn't enter a single Muslim house to either take somebody out or to let rip on them. I don't know this woman by the name, so I would really be curious to know how come she knew my name, given that 90 per cent of the people in town didn't know my name. They only knew my nickname. And now you're talking about a 65-year-old woman who knew that was me. And I claim that I never entered a single Muslim house to either bring somebody out of it or to beat them up or ill treat them in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, before the war you and SOS group waged a campaign of terror and intimidation, blowing up building belonging to non-Serbs. During the war you took part in cleansing operations, you destroyed religious monuments, you appropriated Muslim property. And then when in September 1995 Arkan and his men came to Sanski Most, you helped them round up local Muslims and you handed them over to detention and, in many instances, to their death. Now, you were intimately involved in the crimes that were occurring in Sanski Most, and it is in your personal interest to lie about those crimes and your role in them. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat: We did not commit crimes. We did not assist Arkan when he came. We did not blow up buildings. All the statements went through myself and Saovic, and if anybody was not clear on something, it would have been either Mudrinic or Saovic. I can't agree with what it says here, that we intimidated people. The 5- or 6.000 people who remained in Sanski Most came to look for us, to help them if there was even a -- the slightest provocation. In any case, we helped everybody. We did not abduct anybody. We did not take anybody out of their house or beat them or ill treat them in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. McKenna. Mr. Karadzic do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, we will start with last things first. In the statement 26034, the person says that in 1995, in the zone, there were only 30 per cent Muslims. How does this tally with your experience? Did she overestimate the figure or underestimate it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I did not understand your question. What --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I object to this question because it is not related to the topic that we dealt with in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor claims that Muslims were either expelled or being expelled, and this person here in the statement said there were 30 per cent in 1995, and that she herself lived in the house with her husband in 1995. I'm asking the witness were they expelled and if they were, indeed, how come the 30 per cent that remained living there were not expelled.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody was expelled. And the 30 per cent that remained -- when we're talking about per cent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, question was not yet asked. But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll allow you to continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to what you knew or according to your estimate, how many Muslims lived in Sanski Most in September 1995? Here, in the statement, we see 30 per cent. Do you think that there were more or less?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I believe that there were about 5.000 Muslims. I don't know how many that would be in percentages because I don't know how many were there before the war. But I believe there were about 5.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the decisive factor for some of them to stay living in Sanski Most or -- and the others to leave, was it expulsion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: No, there were no expulsion drives. Those who wanted to stay, they stayed. And those who wanted to leave, they left. There were a lot of troops in Sanski Most, coming from all sides, and when various municipalities fell, people withdrew from those municipalities and then a -- Muslims started expressing their wish to leave Sanski Most and to go to third countries. Some of them had sent their children away first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 9, you were asked whether your nickname is Medeni. Since many participants in the trial do not speak the Serbian language, could you please tell us whether that nickname means something in the Serbian language? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: This means sweet or honey-bunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is derived from the word "honey"; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't sound cruel to me, does it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: It's not cruel, no. No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 43, you said that (redacted) was in prison in Bihac. Whose prison was that and why?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If I may interrupt. I believe that we might need to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Perhaps the name can be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You spoke about a person who was in Bihac in prison. Whose prison was that? And why was the person there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, he lived with us. We had grown up together. We had attended school together. And when we left Sanski Most, he left with us. The Muslims looked for him. They knew his name. They wanted to learn about us because he had been with us all the time. He slept with us. He was a very honest guy. And then the Muslims from Sanski Most started looking for him to be exchanged. He expressed a wish to remain living in Prijedor with us. But he eventually went there, and as far as I heard, he was interrogated there. He was sent to the prison in Bihac. There he was interviewed again. He was ill-treated, he was beaten, but then he was released. I heard from a Muslim friend who came to Banja Luka, after he was released from prison, for four or five months he drunk heavily and he died five or six months later. In any case, he was in the prison in Bihac and that prison was under Muslim control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 40, you were asked about cars which were confiscated. Who was it who confiscated them and why?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all the unnecessary microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The cars were confiscated by individuals from Muslims. Why, I don't know on what grounds. I don't know on what grounds they were confiscated. However, most of those cars were gifted to friends, to Serbian friends, by Muslims, to avoid those cars falling into disrepair or something. In a majority of the cases, if the Muslim who gifted the car to somebody had to be helped or if somebody had to be taken to hospital or if he needed any assistance, that could be arranged. It was all based on arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the cars which were driven by SOS members? Who had confiscated them and on what grounds? Did the police confiscate cars from both Serbs and Muslims and on what grounds?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Cars were, indeed, confiscated. The police did confiscate cars. If somebody changed their mind, the police would then return the car to the Muslims who had changed his mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 39 it was suggested that you were given business premises as gifts. Were the business premises gifted to you or was there any contract? And what was the wording in the contracts?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor did mention several shops, and I know about those three first shops that there was a contract drafted by a lawyer, and that person who -- who was involved was sitting next to me. And when it comes to the other shops, allegedly, they were auctioned off by the municipality. I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were those private shops or socially owned shops?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
