utterances.text: They were -- I apologise. There were also socially owned shops which were held by people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about your contract, did you sign it as a member of the SOS or as a private individual?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I signed it as a private individual, and the person who co-signed it was my very good friend. And the whole thing was done on his initiative. And after that, he continued being a patron of that shop, until the moment he decided to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 23 -- and I don't know whether it was in private session or not. It wasn't because the person testified in open court. You were shown Adil Draganovic's statement. He was the president of the court in Sanski Most before the war. And you said that he may have been involved in crimes. Who was he? Who was that person? Would you say that his testimony against the Serbs in Sanski Most was objective?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Adil worked at the court at that time too. I don't know if I can say this, but he was not very popular among people. He was not popular with me, that's sure. I was informed by the court in Sanski Most, to my address, that a ban has been placed on me regarding the sale of real estate. And in that ban, it is written that Nedeljko Rasula, the wife of late Saovic, and myself, and one Professor Bosko Banjac should collect 100.000 Deutschmark to give him, and then he, as the president of the court, will lift that ban on the sale of real estate from us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown D4174.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that he was perhaps involved in some criminal dealings. Was it extortion -- this extortion of 100.000 Deutschmark the only crime he was involved in or did you hear about other things?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this, please. Can you tell us under whose control and where is Buzim, and the public prosecutor's office there, under whose control was it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I believe it was under the control of Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which ethnic community?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now please look down below, criminal reports and decisions of the municipal court after the war are listed, (c), it says: Pursuant to the decision of the municipal court, ordered an unauthorised payment of 1.000 [as interpreted] Deutschemark to the benefit of the Islamic religious community of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we turn the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, it says he embezzled from the budget of Buzim 187.961 Deutschmark. Does that sound like him?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Well, if he asked us do collect and give him 100.000 German marks, then this sounds plausible. It's probably correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of man was he when it came to political issues and resolving the crisis? Why was he brought into custody? Why was he treated as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: He was extreme in his views. And he was inclined to these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was Sarcevic Ismet, Sabic Suad, Mirzet Karabeg, what were these people like?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I don't see how this comes from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can restrict myself to Mirzet Karabeg. That does emanate from the cross.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Karabeg was an extremist and that's probably why he was taken into custody and questioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly show D5 to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Can we go back to the previous document. D4174. You answered to Mr. Karadzic that this prosecutor's office was under the control of Muslim community. Can we see the last page? It's written by a gentleman -- a Zlatko Pozderac. Can you tell us about the ethnicity of this author?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about this family, Pozderac? Were they well-known?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: They are well-known mostly by a former official from that family, Hamdija Pozderac.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly show D5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 27 -- sorry, 7 March 1992, an operative officer of the state security, the joint state security, writes about extremists in Sanski Most who are procuring weapons for the Green Berets, and among them are Adil Draganovic and Mirzet Karabeg. How is this consistent with what you know?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Well, from what I know, these two did do these things, and they were the most extreme people in the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 18 of today's LiveNote, it is said that allegedly in 1992, you used to go to the barracks in Prijedor and brought back weapons. My first question is: Did the SOS in Sanski Most exist before that date on the proclamation of their establishment in Lusci Palanka?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Second, were you part of the Territorial Defence of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The distribution of JNA weapons from the barracks to the Territorial Defence men, was it legal or not? It doesn't matter whether you did it or not.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: It is not illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In one of those statements - I want to avoid closing the session - it is said that in September 1995 and throughout the war, whatever was done was done on the orders of the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most. Do you know how long the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most existed? When was it abolished?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know the year? Did it exist in 1995, the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: No. Because the state of war had already been declared. It did not exist. I don't think it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the document that was recently admitted, P6682, page 15, it is said that as of 18 June 1992, you were no longer called SOS but you were called instead the sabotage or intervention platoon. Why were you no longer called SOS?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Because we were inducted into the 4th Sana Brigade as the intervention platoon of the 6th Sana Brigade, but the people were already used in their minds to seeing us and calling us SOS. Although, from that time on, we were really the intervention battalion of the 6th Sana Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before they joined the SOS, were some of its members already notorious or convicted criminals? I'm talking about after they joined.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: There were no criminals among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And my last question: Were you the only group that was called SOS? And what is the core of your disagreements with the authorities?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, there was another group also called SOS but we had absolutely no connection to them. The Croatian armed forces had already been formed, and the Muslim armed forces as well, so we just picked a name for ourselves: Serbian Defence Forces. Similar to HOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it the Serb Armed Forces or the Serb Defence Forces, SOS, both?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Serb Defence Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there anyone else in Sanski Most with the same name? And did you have to prove to the authorities who is who?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: Not -- there was no one else in Sanski Most called that way, but there were cases when somebody else represented themselves falsely as SOS, committing robberies and looting. But then we called the president of the municipality and the commander of the Territorial Defence, and we took them to the premises where we were quartered. We gave them a list of all the young men who were there. They were able to see that the men had stayed in that hall. And the president of the municipality and the commander of the TO got into the car together and drove to the Muslim part of the town and found people with tractors -- tractors and wheel-barrows who had written "SOS" on these vehicles and committed robberies and looted, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I'd like to ask just one question related to the topic of the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And which -- related to which?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The ban on real estate imposed by Mr. Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, you talked about the ban on the sale of real estate placed on you, Mr. Rasula, and Mr. Saovic. That ban was because Mr. Draganovic was taking a civil action against you and the other people named based on an allegation that you and Njunja had set his house on fire on the 27th of May, 1992, by firing shells from a cannon at the house. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: That is not true. In this statement, in fact, in this judgement of the court imposing a ban on me, I had read that his house had been sets on fire, that it had been torched by the Black George Platoon. And he mentioned my name as part of that Black George Platoon as the person who fired a gun. Whereas there was another person who had the same truck in Lusci Palanka. He connected me in this statement with this Black George Platoon and, furthermore, he claimed that I fired that gun. I did not fire that gun. I was not the gunner, and I wasn't even on that truck. I was not an infantryman. I was not able to fire. If Black George indeed fired, that's possible. I don't know. But in his statement he mentioned the triple-barrelled gun, Black George, and myself, whereas we had nothing to do with each other. That's what's written in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: But just to clarify, the ban on real estate that he imposed on you was related to his allegations that you were involved in the shelling of his house. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I'm trying to explain to you now. In his statement, he's talking about a gun called Black George firing at his house and torching it. And he places me in the same context as this Black George gun, whereas I had nothing to do with that gun. I mentioned already there were two trucks of the same kind in the brigade. If he mentioned the Black George --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mudrinic, I'm obviously not being clear. Leaving aside the issue of whether you had anything to do with it, the reason that he imposed a ban on your sale of real estate was because he alleged that you were involved. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MUDRINIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. That's not true. I'm telling you again: In the court verdict that I received imposing a ban on me in the sale of properties, it is written that I had torched his house using the Black George gun. Whereas I had nothing to do, no contact with that Black George gun mounted on top of a truck, and I never targeted his house. Because of all this, I hired a lawyer who went to court in Sanski Most and they transferred the case to the court in Bihac, and later on, to Bosanska Krupa, and that lawyer managed to get the case out. And people wondered how he had managed but, in fact, the lawyer had explained to me that if we collect 100.000 Deutschmark, the case would be dismissed. And that happened three or four years later.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mudrinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: That concludes my --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellency, may I only one clarification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: About what, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: About the criminal proceeding, whether it was official or private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Criminal proceedings? It's an injunction in civil proceedings. That ban was done pursuant to a court order. That's what you are saying. Whatever the reason it might have been. Do you agree, Mr. Mudrinic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But after that, although there was a lawsuit perhaps, when the lawyer managed to get that ban lifted, I wasn't kept informed all the time but in -- in the end, my lawyer explained it to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant to ask if the public prosecutor had ever issued an indictment, ex officio, in this matter against the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I wasn't informed about it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That concludes your evidence, Mr. Mudrinic. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for coming to The Hague to give it. You're now free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I -- before we continue, I think I need to come back to the intercept issue. There seems to have been a misunderstanding on my part, and I was confused. So I -- I -- my understanding was that the Prosecution was not minded to object or actually agree to the -- to the authenticity of the bunch of Croatian intercepts that were the subject of the forthcoming witness, but it was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm -- apologise. It was obviously not sufficiently clear on that. Your current understanding is right, that was not the case. We have not agreed on that. I think Mr. Robinson proposed to withdraw -- basically to withdraw the motion and move forward. That does seem to make sense. I just hope we're not confusing witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case we do not have to wait for your response. You don't need to respond at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Exactly. And that's something Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff mentioned at the break, but we thought there might be other reasons why the Court wanted some feedback. But I think your position is quite correct and that is the position we all thought was going to be taken, and as I mentioned, Mr. Robinson suggested that explicitly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then you will go ahead with calling that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that date is planned on your part on 3rd of March, Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I was suggesting that we do it at 4.00 on the 3rd of March, interrupt Dr. Karadzic's testimony so that it doesn't take place at the beginning of that day when the public is expecting to hear Dr. Karadzic and we're all in closed session dealing with an intercept issue. So I thought it would be better if we scheduled it at 4.00, but it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there would be no -- you're not making any observation --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we break or continue with the next witness -- oh, we have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gruban.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Gruban, I must let you know a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the Tribunal. That is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any case except the -- save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Gruban.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you to leave a pause before -- between questions and answers. You enunciate very well. I'm just asking you to speak slowly to save time and save ourselves the trouble with transcript. Have you given a statement to my Defence team, Mr. Gruban?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 1D9652.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the left-hand side, do you see the first page of the Serbian version of your statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: I have both read and signed it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us display the last page so the witness can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you've stated to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put to you the same questions today, would your answers be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes, they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this package under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. We have designated 23 photographs as associated exhibits. They're not on our 65 ter list because we hadn't taken the statement from the witness at the time this list was filed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Do you have any objections, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit them all.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The statement, 1D9652, will be Exhibit D4388. And 24 photographs will be Exhibits D4389 through to Exhibits D4412, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll hear the summary after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: As you like it, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll break for 45 minutes, and resume at five past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.21 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the remainder of today and tomorrow, we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis in the absence of Judge Lattanzi, who cannot be with us due to her personal matters. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out in English a short summary of the statement of Mr. Momcilo Gruban. I will then ask him to explain to us two documents that he was kind enough to bring along. [In English] Momcilo Gruban was mobilised in September 1991 into the reserve police forces, where he remained till the end of the war. He arrived at the Omarska Collection and Investigation Centre in early June 1992 and was appointed to be the security shift leader. In 2008/2009, the Chamber of the BH Court convicted him to seven years in prison. On 31st of December, 2010, he was released on probation. After the outbreak of conflict in the territory of Prijedor municipality, Mr. Gruban was engaged in the Omarska police squad. He operated in the territory of Maricka local commune, which comprised some 15 houses inhabited by residents of other ethnicities. None of them were killed or had their property destroyed, and these people still live in the territory of Maricka local commune. The detainees in the Omarska Collection and Investigation Centre were people who had been found in the combat zone and had been brought in there in order to clarify their involvement in the armed conflict. Their detention was to be temporary and, once their responsibility was established, they were to be released or to be sent to one of the prisons. The detainees were held in several rooms, and they were categorised by inspectors of the military, state, and security -- public security. The Territorial Defence had the task of securing the outer ring around the mine compound, while the reserve police formation of Omarska was in charge of providing security within the Omarska Collection and Investigation Centre. In the first three weeks since the establishment of the centre, security was also provided by the special police units of the Banja Luka Security Service Centre, CSB. The tasks of Mr. Gruban included the maintenance of communications and the distribution of meals to the guards, as well as reporting to the head of the police part of the security, Mr. Mejakic, about the information received during his shift. Mr. Gruban's shift composed about 20 police officers armed with long barrels of various calibres. In the absence of any concrete orders regarding the treatment of detainees, they agreed to help these men as much as possible within their power. During Mr. Gruban's shift, the conditions of stay were as humane as possible in the circumstances of the state of war and general penury. The detainees were -- had access to water, toilets, and they did not fear ill-treatment. A total of about 2.500 detainees passed through Omarska, of which about 30 were women who had been active in the armed rebellion. The accommodation capacity was appropriate at the beginning, but as an increasing number of detainees kept arriving, it soon became insufficient and a number of detainees were sent outdoors during the day but could spend the night in the restaurant. Mr. Gruban did not see any persons younger than 15, nor did he see any mentally impaired individuals at the Omarska Investigation Centre. The regulation stipulated that when a person was being accepted in any detention facility, they were to be searched. No ill-treatment was allowed in the procedure, and Mr. Gruban did his best to prevent it. A special group of police officers was designated to bringing -- for bringing the detainees to questioning and then taking them back to their rooms. Sometimes inspectors raised their voices during interrogations, and in some case, physical force was applied; but in most cases, the detained persons themselves recognised that the interrogation had been correct. The detainees could eat meals at their ease, and most of them went regularly to queue up for the distribution of food. Nonetheless, the extremists who had participated in the attack on Prijedor and had been wounded in combat were detained in the white house, and their food was brought to them by other detainees. Water was available to the prisoners, and most rooms had several taps. The complex of the mine was supplied with drinking water from two deep wells before and during the war. The precarious hygiene conditions were a result of the war-time circumstances, and there was no planned ill-treatment of the detainees. There were some cases of individual armed groups outside the system of authority that managed to get in the Omarska and ill-treated the detainees. These paramilitary groups were well armed, so the guards at the centre were not able to resist them because the police officers were deployed across the whole complex, which covered a very large area. Mr. Gruban did not -- is not aware of any case of rape, assault, or humiliation of prisoners. To his knowledge, no one was targeted on the basis of their education or religion or other affiliation. And that is short summary. Now I would ask Mr. Gruban about the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, you have kindly brought us two documents which are connected with your statement and your line of duty. Please explain to us what it is about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 1D49067. We only need one. And can it be enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you help us, Mr. Gruban, tell us what is this that we are looking at? And who drew it and who wrote the notes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Well, we see the ground floor of the administration building of the Omarska mine, where people were detained. I myself wrote the notes because I was working there, and I was fully familiar with the premises. I can tell you exactly where the people stayed, and I even know the area surface. In preparation for my testimony, I drew this up because I wanted to show to all the parties in the proceedings, including the Judges, what the actual situation was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what does A1 stand for, A2, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: A1 is the garage which was intended for the official vehicle. It's got 21.16 square metres. 4.60 by 4.60 metres are the dimensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't have to go into that much detail. Just let us know what the rooms were used for, and then as your testimony goes along, we'll clarify this. Can you explain this further?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: A3 were the five booths with toilets and four urinals. A4, we had ten water taps. A5 is the entranceway in the administrative building on the eastern side. A6 depicts five booths on each side with showers. A7 and A8 are all rooms equipped with showers, so there's a total of 25 in all. 25 showers in this area. Before the war, the rooms were used by the workers in the Omarska surface mine. AD is the area where they had their lockers, where the dressing room was. And, of course, the showers were for them to clean themselves at the end of their shift before they went to home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thanks. What is A22?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: A22 is the canteen, the dining hall. 243 square metres is the surface --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the dimensions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As workers we would have our meals here. Later on, when the detainees were held here, this is where their meals would be distributed to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A19 again we see taps and toilets mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes. It is like an ante-chamber to the dining hall, where one could use the toilet facilities and water taps to wash their hands. When the detainees were here, in A19, there were medical nurses there, and they used certain -- some sort of a chlorine solution or something like that that people had to dowse themselves with to prevent any sort of infection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Line 8, witness said: "AD is the area where they had their lockers." I can't find AD in the schematic -- in the schematic. Yes, Mr. Gruban.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's A9. The large room that you can see. A9, not D.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: In Serbian, 9 is devet, with D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have any instances of infection spreading or epidemics while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: I know of one case involving a person. I can't tell you what the disease was. But we had a nurse present there. At this time, there was a shortage of fuel. Since I had been employed in the mine and I was familiar with the machinery, I went to one of these pieces of machinery, decanted the fuel in order to take the individual to the hospital in Banja Luka. He was hospitalised there, treated, and is alive and well, thank God, and we are still in contact today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please speak slowly. What is number 14?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Number 14 is a glazed-in area, like a conservatory, outside the entrance to the building, and prisoners were also held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about number 15? Did we confuse the two?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Number 15 is the entrance from the south into the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where is the kitchen? Can we see it from here?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: You mean the conveyor belt for the distribution of food. Food were delivered in tin plates into 28, and 23 was the conveyor line. That was the same before the war and during the time when people were held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How about the use of this building before the war, before detainees were held there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes. It was the building of the mine. It was first used during the war to keep detainees, and then later Serbian troops and Serbian refugees from Sanski Most, Drvar, Petrovac, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the building repaired, maintained, renovated between the time when detainees were held there and the time when Serbian troops and refugees were held?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: No. The first reconstruction was in 2004, when company Mittal took the mine over. The facade and -- and the outside structure was repaired a bit but nothing was done in the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where does this company Mittal come from?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: It's a very well-known company that produces iron-ore. They have ironworks and steelworks. They own Cicak and Smederevo ironworks, and they have other branches and properties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said an Indian person is the owner, and it's a British company?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, did you have any better, more comfortable premises to place these prisoners or, rather, detainees who were to be questioned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, there was no such place in the area of Prijedor municipality that could house so many detainees. In the centre of the public security station, there was one small detention room where a few people could be kept but not even ten people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what we see here?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: This sketch, this plan, shows one floor, one of the upper floors, of the administration building. The -- the one before was the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What are these rooms that are marked? And what is the area that is unmarked?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: They were used before the war. I indicated here who occupied these rooms. The administrator, the typists. In -- number 9, there were accountants and bookkeepers. And there was a large conference room. B1 was the office of the director. B2, secretary. B1, director. B4, lawyer. B5, mining engineers. Then there were toilets and bathrooms. Each one had a shower. B8 was the hallway, et cetera. That was before the relevant events. However, when this all happened, these rooms on the upper floor of the administration building were used by teams of inspectors made up of three men each who questioned the detainees, made a selection, categorisation, et cetera. There was a room, a duty service room, which had a radio station, two typists who typed up the statements made by the detainees on the old-type typewriters, the classical typewriters. There were no computers at the time, and these statements were later returned to be signed, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see the ERN number. Who made this sketch, the markings apart from yours made in pencil?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: I received this from the OTP. Everything that we were able to receive in our case, all the documents and records, we received all that thanks to the OTP, because we were unable to get hold of any of it. You know when the SFOR took over the security documentation, we were no longer able to get anything from there without the help of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is this large unmarked space?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: It's part of the roof shown from the top, from above. Over the refectory.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page. In line 8, it should say that it is the roof above the refectory, above the canteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We saw the canteen in the first sketch; right? What is this? Can you help us.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: This is the ground floor of the work-shop which was often mentioned in court as the hangar. It's used by the OTP. It was a work-shop used before the war to maintain various excavators and construction machines for the purposes of the mine. And when the events began, detainees were held here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What do we see down here? A bathroom?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes, a bathroom. That's room A11. There are 24 wash-basins, dozens of urinals, et cetera. And the detainees were kept in this area in the left top corner. You see 23 metres long and 4 and a half metres wide. That's where the prisoners were. And on the ground floor, there's another room which housed prisoners. If you can see A17. That's about the ground floor. And from the ground floor, you have two staircases. It's A8 and another one. Do you see where I'm pointing? A15 and A8, those were stairs that led to the upper floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next picture?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the upper floor of the work-shop?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's the upper floor. So left to those from the stairs. This large room, I didn't get the picture at that time, I got it later from the OTP, but when I was preparing, I drew it this way. This large room marked at as A1, that's where detainees were placed --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, can you tell us what it used to be before?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: It used to be a big conference room for the people in the work-shop who worked in maintenance, like I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: A2, it used to be the office of the administrator. It was emptied. All the furniture was removed, like it was removed from all the other rooms. A3 and A4 were also used to house detainees. And there are two bathrooms. I marked them as 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is shown here? What did it used to be? And how was it used during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: So when you get to the upper floor, the first picture we saw showed the area on the left, and this picture shows the area to the right of the stairs. And this is marked, for instance, let's begin with number 4. That was the wardrobe, the cloak-room where people changed. However when the detainees arrived --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: When the detainees came all these cupboards were removed, and detainees were placed in that area. The room I marked with a 6 were showers for the workers who worked on maintenance. That's where they had showers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please slow down. It was showers for workers. But during the detention time, how was it used?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: The detainees were housed in all these rooms. None of the security men or the guards went into those areas. The guards were standing around the stairs leading to this upper floor. So the detainees were free to use this whole space. Look at room 15. It used to be the car mechanics' electrical work-shop. That area was also emptied and prepared to house detainees. Just as all these other small rooms. All the inventory, all the furniture was removed and made available to the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us a bit about the supply of food. What kind of challenge was it for the municipal authorities? How much food was used by this facility?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: You mean when it held detainees?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Food for the detainees was prepared in a kitchen that is about a kilometre and a half away from this facility, in a building which stands at the very entrance to the Omarska mine. There were difficulties, major difficulties, in preparing food, especially when there were power cuts. And the food there was prepared at the same time for the troops, for the police, and the detainees. A very large number of meals was prepared there. Detainees received one meal per day that contained a plateful of cooked food and a piece of bread. But generally speaking, in the area of Omarska in Krajina, we were cut off from the rest of the world. The corridor was blocked. Krajina was completed encircled. There were great deficits of food and medicines, and if you remember in Banja Luka, 12 babies were -- died because medicines could not be supplied to them. Only when Krajina was connected by the corridor with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the rest of Republika Srpska and Bosnia-Herzegovina did it become possible to deliver food, medicines, and other necessities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The transcript refers to a piece of bread, whereas you said a quarter of a kilo, 250 grams.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes, a quarter of a loaf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Plus some of us brought food from our homes and distributed it among the detainees. We did that at our own initiative, and I'm not the only one who did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4413, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Another document is a list of populated areas, but we can dispense with it now because it's not a priority. Thank you. I have nothing further at this time.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: If you allow me, I'm not sure when you were reading the statement, there were some errors. Perhaps it's the interpretation. The interpretation I heard was that I was assigned to be shift leader, where I was actually the duty officer in -- in that room where I worked. And another thing that I heard in interpretation was the chief was Mejakic. Mejakic was not the chief. I'm sorry, I don't know whether it's wrongly recorded or it's just misinterpreted but we all know that Mejakic was not the chief. And there's another mistake that I noted down, namely that detainees were able to eat as they wished. It is not exactly so. They could eat when their turn came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Gruban [as interpreted] is said to be here -- to be head of one part of the police security. Maybe you received a different interpretation. In any case, thank you for these explanations. And this summary of your statement is not in evidence. What matters is what we read in the official witness statement. Do you have the witness statement before you? Because you will now be cross-examined. Do you have it on paper?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 14, it says "Gruban" whereas it should read "Mejakic." Because it is for Mejakic that the short summary states that he was the head of the civilian police part. I said "Mejakic," and the record reads "Gruban."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, you were also known as Momo Gruban; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your nickname is Ckalja; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were publicly indicted in February 1995 by this Tribunal and you remained a fugitive until your surrender in May 2002; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: The indictment was issued -- I was not a fugitive. I responded to the invitation of the Tribunal as soon as the Law on Co-operation was adopted between the Republika Srpska and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. At the time I was in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and as soon as those two legal documents were adopted, I responded to the Tribunal's summons immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were at large between February 1995 and May 2002; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. It was interpreted you were at large or free, I believe that "at large" means to be a fugitive. We should ask the witness what he thinks and whether he confirms any of the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, he has answered the question. He said yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He raised the issue of interpretation. He heard as -- the question as asking whether he was free. Line 17. If you could ask the question again, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, you remained at large, or you were free, you didn't surrender yourself to the Tribunal when you were publicly indicted in May -- in February 1995 and you remained a free person until May 19 -- 2002, I'm sorry, when you surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: I could not surrender because the authorities of my own state had not adopted the Law on Co-operation. Some people surrendered along private lines. Let me remind you, when I arrived in The Hague, Mr. Kwon was a member of the Chamber as well as the late May and Judge Robinson. I was the first Serb who was provisionally released against the guarantees of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Republika Srpska, and I complied all of the conditions on which I was provisionally released and that resulted in the provisional release of all the other detainees, which means when I was provisionally released, I complied with all the conditions of that decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, that was unresponsive to my question. I asked you nothing about provisional release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In 2006 your case was transferred from the ICTY to the BiH state court where you were tried along with remaining co-accused with Zeljko Mejakic, Dusko Knezevic, and Dusan Fustar; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Not correct. Zeljaja was not with me. We were not on the same case. I have not heard that before. I was transferred to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Gruban, I said Zeljko Mejakic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Let me tell you the -- the debate on our transfer to the court in Sarajevo was held here. My Defence and myself objected because we thought that we wouldn't have a fair trial in Sarajevo and that our human rights would be violated there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, I'm sorry to interrupt you. I simply asked you to confirm that in 2006 your case was transferred from here to the state court and you were tried with the three people I named. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Unfortunately, unfortunately, the cases were transferred.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you were tried and convicted in 2008 of crimes committed against non-Serbs in the Omarska camp. You were convicted of crimes against humanity, for crimes committed on your shift and also for crimes committed outside your shift in furtherance of the system of ill-treatment and persecution at the camp; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I should have been rewarded for what I did and the way I behaved. However, the court that we have just discussed violated the human rights of the accused. My file is still in Strasbourg. The Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina also quashed the judgements due to the retroactive application of the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, you were convicted of crimes against humanity by the state court; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Unfortunately, you saw how the court acted. The decision was what it was. But this is still not final. I hope that the court in Strasbourg will quash the decision and that it will return the case for retrial.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were specifically convicted of murder; imprisonment, that is, arbitrary and unlawful confinement of camp detainees; torture, which was beatings and other physical assaults; sexual violence, which was rapes and other forms of sexual abuse; persecution; and other inhumane acts, which was the confinement of the detainees in inhumane condition -- inhuman conditions, harassment, humiliation, and other psychological abuse. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: This is what you say. Investigations were carried against me from the moment the first prisoners were released in 1992 until the very end. I have not come across a single statement of a single witness who would have stated that I committed a wrong-doing against any of the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, I'm asking you to confirm that those were the crimes that you were convicted of by the Bosnian State Court. Now, as I announced them, that was the finding of your trial chamber, yes? Whether you agree with it or not that was the decision -- that was the finding of your chamber. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: I've just told you that the trial is still ongoing. My appeal has been filed with the court in Strasbourg. That may well be the case at the moment, but I certainly hope that this will not be the final decision on this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you were originally sentenced to a term of imprisonment of 11 years which was reduced on appeal to seven years; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 of your statement, you said that the Serbs held a majority in 42 of 72 settlements in Prijedor municipality. The Serbs were not the majority population in the Prijedor municipality. There were more Muslims than Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: According to the 1999 census, for the first time ever there were more Muslims than Serbs in Prijedor. And of the 71 settlements, Serbs were a majority in 42 settlements or 67 per cent of the overall territory of Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Nor were the Serbs the majority population in the Prijedor town when you add the ethnicities, the Muslim and the Croat ethnicities, together?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Serbs accounted for a majority in the town of Prijedor. If you have the 1991 census, and I received it from you, you will see that, according to that census, Serbs had a majority in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In Prijedor town, there were 13.927 Serbs. And if you combine the Muslim and Croat population, you have a population of 15.145. Do you -- we can bring up the census, but do you take my word for those figures? In Prijedor town, I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: I don't know why you combine Muslims and Croats. Why do you think that they are a whole? What about Yugoslavs and others? What category do you think that they should fall under?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, if we add them as well, then you come to a total of 20.708. So the Serbs weren't in a majority in Prijedor town; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Serbs accounted for a majority in comparison with all the other individual categories. I mean Muslims, Croats, Yugoslavs, and -- and others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, you said that Maricka local commune comprised of some 15 houses inhabited by about 50 residents of other ethnicities, and you mentioned it again in your testimony today. There were, in fact, five Croats and no Muslims living in the village of Maricka, were there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Where did you find that? If you have the census, put it on the screen, and you will see that there were 50 non-Serbs, which is the term that you've been using here. 50 non-Serbs who throughout the war lived in the area, they still live there. None of them was killed. They still have their property, their religious buildings, their cemeteries. Nothing has changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, there were five Croats, no Muslims, one Yugoslav, and 28 other ethnicities in the village of Maricka. Do you confirm that there were -- do you agree with me when I say there were only five Croats and no Muslims? And that's according to the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we are talking at cross-purposes. The local commune of Maricka consists of three Maricka: Upper, lower, and middle Maricka, and the village of Krivaja. Those four villages constitute the local commune of Maricka, Krivaja, and the villages that go by the same name, Maricka. So that's what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you agree that in that commune there were only five Croats and no Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Why is it a problem? Put the census on the screen. Let's not speculate. I know that there were 50. Why should we speculate? Let's make thing really clear by showing the census.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: We could offer this document to be uploaded, to be shown, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The 65 ter number is 00242S, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, excuse me, Mr. Karadzic. I'm calling up the 1991 census published in Zagreb in 1995 and that's 65 ter number 00242S, which is the data for Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in 1995, there was no census. There was one in 1991 and then the next one was organised last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you can deal with it in your re-examination, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to the second --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, you can see there down the bottom it starts: "Prijedor municipality." Iliskic [phoen], Babici, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, it is generally known that the census took place in 1991 and then last year. I've never heard of the 1995 census before. Who was it who carried out this census? How -- my name is not there. I was not -- not aware of the 1995 census.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Clearly I said it's the 1991 census which was published in 1995. So this is the 1991 census. If we can turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. There, down the bottom, the third from the bottom we see Maricka. And that is -- if we go to the very right-hand column we can see that is just numbered number 43 so that when we go to the following page --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: I apologise. Can the letters and figures be zoomed in just a little. They're a bit too small for me to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now you see number 43 and you see there's 1.598 Serbs, 5 Croats, no Muslims, 1 Yugoslav, and 28 other people.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes. But what about the other figures? I can't see the top of those columns. Then can you scroll down? I can see that there are Yugoslavs, Serbs ... two Yugoslavs; right? If I'm supposed to be looking at line 43.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: One Yugoslav and 28 others. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, I'm not sure if I'm following this correctly. Can we see the upper part of this page? Do we see two 1991s?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in English translation, we see the years 1948, 1953, 1961, 1971, and 1981.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's on the previous page, Your Honour. The census is always two pages for every page [sic]. Two pages for every settlement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you like to pursue this issue, why don't you print out those two pages and offer the printout to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, if that can be done.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be heard, I'm going to read the title in Serbian and I want it to be interpreted. "The population of Croatia which hails from Bosnia and Herzegovina" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have English translation. I think it's being printed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Mr. Gruban, when you get this piece of paper, I'm interested in the figures on the left-hand side of the page. Now I simply want you to confirm that there were in fact only five Croats and no Muslims in the commune of Maricka.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: I'm really confused because the title says: "The population of Croatia which hails from Bosnia-Herzegovina segregated by settlements." Besides, on page 197 I don't have any settlements, I just have figures. So based on the figures, I don't know the exact number of the population. Look at the first page. You see the names of the settled places. Do you have something similar to this? Do you have where it says Maricka, Krivaja, and the figures, and then I would able to actually draw a conclusion about the exact figure and data. You see here, there's no name of the place here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, as I showed you initially when it was on the screen, you saw Maricka on the third line up from the bottom. We also saw that it was number 43 over on this right-hand corner -- side of the page. So when you go over the page, you look at number 43 and you see the continuing data for 1991. Total Croats, Muslims, Serbs, Yugoslavs, and other.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Please. Since you're talking about that, add Krivaja to that because Krivaja is also a part of that local commune. I was talking about the local commune of Maricka, not the settlement of Maricka. This is what you will find in my statement. And then you will do your maths and will you see that the sum should be around 50.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this and move on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Two pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. It's the -- the census data for the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How many pages? Six pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we should look at the official census from the official state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm confused with the page number. Are you tendering how many pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Six, Your Honour. It may be easier to look at the hard copy that was printed by the usher to see the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll -- we don't need to MFI it. We can admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6684, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, in paragraph 2 of your statement you say that the Serbs owned 67 per cent of the territory and that the non-Serb minorities in this area enjoyed the protection of the authorities and most still live there. Now you know that this isn't true. The non-Serb minorities did not enjoy the protection of the authorities and most of them do not live there.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: I can speak about the areas where I lived and worked, which is my local commune. All the non-Serbs throughout the war remained living there. Their religious edifices and cemeteries and property were not touched --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, sorry to interrupt you again, but my time is limited. You are limiting that statement in paragraph 2 to only your village; is that right? Not -- not the -- the entire municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: My local commune and the surrounding communes, for example, the villages such as Gradina, Jelicka, Lamovita, Bistrica, Omarska, Sanicani, Rakelici, Busnovi, Tomasica, were villages in the catchment area of my local commune. I was not aware of a single case of somebody having been killed because they were not a Serb or that their property was destroyed or any such thing that may have happened in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You agree with me, don't you, that non-Serb property in parts of the Prijedor municipality, like the Brdo area, the Kozarac area, was destroyed by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: You're talking about the settlements which had Muslim majorities. For example, Kozarac, with its catchment area of some five or six villages, and the area of Brdo. That's where Muslim majorities lived and that's where combat operations took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say "combat operations," you mean when there was the shelling by the VRS forces on those areas, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: There was fierce fighting there, for example, on 24th of May. That's when fighting started in Kozarac. A military column was attacked. A barricade was erected on the road, and the military got the orders to lift the blockade and a soldier, Zgonjanin, was killed in the village Jakupovici, which actually launched combat operations on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 05071, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that a combat operations or fighting started on both sides. That was not recorded. That's on lines 21 through 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Gruban? Did you say so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, here we see an operative, an SNB operative's report, Milos, to the authorities, saying that the situation in the municipality of Prijedor is gradually returning to normal. And this is dated the 28th of May, 1992. "The fighting in the Kozarac area is coming to an end and most of the places are held by the Army of the Serbian Republic of BiH. Our forces have lost five men and about ten have been wounded. Whereas, according to fairly reliable sources, it is estimated that enemy losses amount to several hundred men." This wasn't fierce fighting between the two sides. This was a shelling attack on a civilian population that resided in Kozarac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to comment on this document. I think I see it for the first time. I don't know who this Milos is and to whom he belonged. I was in the police at the time; I wasn't in the army. So it's difficult for me to discuss these military operations because I'm not qualified. I know that there was fighting, that that there was reporting and media coverage on both TV and the radio, and you could even hear very loud gun-fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This was in fact the situation, wasn't it? The VRS, as of the 28th of May, 1992, had lost approximately five men and that -- of the Muslim population, the enemy losses amounted to several hundred men. That was the situation and -- and everybody knew that, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm really speculating now. I don't know whether there were five dead and ten wounded and how many there were on the other side. It would be just speculation. I wasn't there. I don't think I should talk about this. You must have had witnesses who could have spoken about it with more basis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just have a clarification. Does this document say that there were losses among the population as stated in line 3? Does the document itself say that the population suffered losses?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I just rise on because this happens repeatedly. This cannot be a serious question by the accused who can read the document. It is obviously a signal to the witness and he should be reprimanded. It's completely inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was checking whether Ms. Sutherland referred to population. Yes ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 93.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, line 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document itself does not refer to population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In that regard, he has a point of objection. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6685, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, you said a moment ago that areas where the Muslim population resided and when -- I mentioned Hambarine and Kozarac but let's talk about in Prijedor. The inhabitants of the old town of Prijedor, also known as Stari Grad, were pre-predominantly persons of Muslim ethnicity. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Old town Prijedor, I did not find it in the census. I don't know where the old town name comes from. Looking at history, Kozarac is older than Prijedor. Prijedor is first mentioned in 1769 as a town. Old town may be a different settlement. I don't think it's in my statement, and I can't understand why the question on this topic arises, but please go on. I don't want you to think that I'm being pathetic. I just don't know what you're trying to get at.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, what I'm getting at is that you stated in paragraph 2 of your statement that non-Serb minorities in the area enjoyed the protection of the authorities and -- and you said most still live there. I'm putting to you that in fact their -- non-Serb property was damaged -- was destroyed by the Serb forces and the Serb authorities. Now you know -- you know the area that I'm talking about that comprises of the Stari Grad settlement, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: I really don't know which settlement in Prijedor is called old town, Stari Grad. Maybe it has a different name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit P03532, please. Now this is a map -- and if we could zoom in a bit further, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We can see just above the river, on the left-hand side of the map, is the area of Stari Grad. It's marked there on the map. Now you know the area that I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can zoom in further.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes, please, what did you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You know the settlement, the Stari Grad settlement that I'm talking about here, you know was completely destroyed by the -- by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: What you call Stari Grad I believe is neighbourhood Bereka. At least that's how we call it. A settlement called Bereka, surrounded by little canals, and it's on the right bank of the Sana river. Is that what you refer to as Stari Grad? I know it as Berek in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. And you know that it was completely destroyed, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: I really don't know that it was completely destroyed. Because at the time of the Muslim forces attack on Prijedor, I was not in that area so I could not talk about it. I was at least 20, 25 kilometres away from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: But I know, I heard when the attack on Prijedor happened --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes, please. So on the 30th of May, there was a mighty attack by Muslim units on the town of Prijedor from several directions. The old hotel was attacked. That force reached the SUP building and the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: The attack began at 4.00 a.m. --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- if I can just interrupt you. My question was directed to this being destroyed and this was destroyed after the attack on Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to get to it. Perhaps we didn't understand each other. What I know is this: The attack lasted around -- until around 11.00. The Serb army and police --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: -- mounted a counter-attack --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- I don't want the details of the attack on Prijedor. The Trial Chamber has heard evidence of that before. I want you to agree with me that the Stari Grad settlement was destroyed after the attack on Prijedor. You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: I don't know that this Stari Grad, or Berek as I know it, was destroyed, but I can tell what you I heard. When these Muslim forces were crushed and began to withdraw, and I know that from the -- their statements and testimony, they pulled out through Stari Grad and from there, allegedly, they put up resistance and the army and police fired at them. And perhaps in the process, some buildings in that area were destroyed. But I'm telling you, that's what I know. I did not see it with my own eyes, and I did not take part. I'm just re-telling what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So if you -- you never passed that settlement ever after -- after the 30th of May to see that was completely destroyed. When you were driving into Prijedor from Maricka, you never, ever, passed the settlement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: This neighbourhood was not on my way. I come to Prijedor from Maricka, Rakelici, Sanicani, Gomjenica, and that's how I arrive at Prijedor and I come from this side. Whereas this neighbourhood is completely on the other side. And it's so kind of in a recess. It's not along the way so you could accidentally pass by or walk into it. You have you to be going there specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to move now to the Omarska camp. You said in paragraph 6 and again today that you were duty officer on one of the shifts. The State Court rejected your claim that you had no command position in the Omarska camp and they -- it concluded that you were one of three guard shift commanders in the Omarska camp; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: I was never appointed as a guards commander. There are different options there. Leaders of the guard, commander of the guards --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban -- Mr. Gruban, please, listen to my question. I said the court reject your claim that you had no command position and the court concluded that were one of three guard shift commanders in the Omarska camp; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: At the very beginning, we talked about that court, how it judged, how it worked, and I don't think it's smart to -- for me to comment on the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You may not agree with it, but that's what the court found; correct? I see you nodding.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Of course, I don't agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But that's what the court found, that you were a shift commander. You were one of the three shift commanders. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Even courts make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, did the court conclude that you were a shift commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that's what the court found. However, as I've said before, it's not over yet, so I don't think I should comment any further. My appeal is before the Strasbourg court. When it's all over, then we can come back to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said in paragraph 8 of your statement that none of the members of the reserve police in your shift ill-treated detainees. Now are you asserting to this Court that crimes didn't occur on your shift?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I assert, and that's correct. If a case like that happened, one of the duty officers or the guards would have been named as the perpetrators of -- of those violations or crimes. So the entire trial, in all of 100 days of trial, not a single guard from my shift was named as a perpetrator of a criminal act.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Trial Chamber found that with respect to your individual criminal responsibility in the Omarska camp, that the system of ill-treatment and persecution included the killing of detainees directly and personally committed by persons during your shift and over whom you had control, including the disappearance in July 1992 of Burhanudin Kapetanovic and a person by the surname of Badnjevic. They also found the shooting of at least 50 detainees from the village of Hambarine in late July 1992. I see you smirking. This is the same incident that you refer to in paragraph 38 of your statement in relation to adjudicated fact 1185, where you state that you have no knowledge of it, therefore it can't be true. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN
utterances.text: Where shall we start? What was your first question? You asked several questions right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
